text:
waku-agent

 Your own AI assistant. On your laptop. In code you can read in an afternoon. 

Meet Waku — a local-first personal assistant that shows the five pillars behind every
serious agent: Harness · Loop · Memory · Eval/LLM-Ops · Always-on . No frameworks hiding the good parts.
Built by seanchen.io.

- Local-first. Your memory is one SQLite file. Open it. Read it. It's yours.
- Memory is the hero. Semantic + episodic + procedural — with a gate that decides whether 
 to remember, and a pass that decides what to keep.
- The loop is 95 lines of plain Python. Step through it.
- Watch it think. A local dashboard lights up every message as it flows through the harness.
- Eval built in. Deterministic tests and LLM-as-judge, side by side, with a release gate.
- Always-on. It sleeps until an event arrives: a message, a timer, your yes. Every event is a
 row on disk first, so a crash loses nothing.

 

 The system-design whiteboard from the series.
 Every box maps to a file — see the architecture.

 Always-on is what happens around a run. Picture the whole chart above as one box called
 "a run": an event inbox and timers wake it, permissions can pause it for your yes, and an outbox
 sends what it decided. The files are in waku/alwayson/ .

 ▶ Watch the series 

- AI Agent Harness & Loop Engineering in 19 min: the concepts behind the first chart.
- The 20-min code walkthrough: the loop, the memory pillars, the evals, the Telegram gateway and the "Waku Waku" wake word, live.

 Waku Memory — the same memory in Claude Code, Codex, Grok Bot and this agent: waku.one · docs

 Now try it. "Remember that Alex prefers morning meetings." Quit. Restart.
 "Book a catch-up with Alex on Friday." → it remembers, and books 9am. Your memory is one
file: /.waku/state.db , the same from every folder.

 Use the model you already pay for. Anthropic (default), OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, MiniMax,

New to it? Getting started walks the whole setup, with a check

 Connect Waku Memory

Waku's own memory is local. Waku Memory is the hosted memory you
share across agents: save something in Claude Code, recall it here.

 

That installs the Waku plugin, the one Claude Code and Codex use. To connect Claude Code, Codex, Hermes or Grok Bot to the
same memory, see integrations.
 For a team. A Waku Memory team space is one memory your whole team's agents write to and
read from: a decision one person's coding agent saves on Monday is there when a teammate, or
Waku in your Slack channel, is asked about it on Friday. Personal memories stay personal; a
person shares one into the team when they choose to.

For live data when it researches, waku connect treg (or /connect treg ) signs in to your own
treg account the same way; see integrations.

 What's inside

 Pillar In one line Read more 
 --- --- --- 
 Harness gateways (terminal, dashboard, voice, Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp) and tools around one loop architecture 
 Loop 95 lines of plain Python: reason, act, repeat, with two ways to stop the tour 
 Memory semantic, episodic and procedural (skills); a gate decides whether to remember, consolidation decides what to keep the tour 
 Eval / LLM-Ops deterministic tests and LLM-as-judge side by side, a release gate, a trace for every turn evals 
 Always-on an event inbox, timers that repeat, runs that pause for your yes, and an outbox that sends once: waku serve integrations 

 How is this different from ChatGPT or Claude Desktop? Those are products you use . This is a
codebase you own : the loop, the memory schema, the gate and the eval harness are all yours to
read and change. Versus the big open-source assistants (OpenClaw, Hermes)? Same architecture,
1/100th the code. And where those are one person's agent, Waku is built to be a teammate: the
same always-on blocks, with a memory a whole team shares.

 Hosted, if you'd rather not run it

agent.waku.one runs the same harness for you: sign in, press
 Add to Slack , and mention @Waku in a channel. It answers in the thread, sets reminders and
a daily brief, and reads Notion, Linear, GitHub and Gmail once you connect them. It reads and
drafts; anything that changes the outside world still needs your yes.

- In a channel it answers from what the team shares. Your personal notes stay out.
- In a private chat it is the same Waku, and there it can use your own memories and mail.
 Today that works for the person who added Waku to the workspace.

It is a preview, invite-only for now. The code is in hosted/ under the
Elastic License, so you can run the whole platform yourself.

install.title: Quickstart
install.html:
Just want to run it:

pip install waku-agent
waku                                    # talk to your Waku in the terminal
waku dashboard                          # …or the browser cockpit → localhost:7777

It will tell you which key to set the first time. No paid key? With OpenRouter, Waku uses free models by default: make a key at openrouter.ai/keys, then run WAKU_PROVIDER=openrouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<your-key> waku. Free models are rate-limited.

Want to read the code (the point of this repo) or contribute — clone it instead:

git clone https://github.com/ShenSeanChen/waku-agent && cd waku-agent
uv venv && uv pip install -e .          # create the env + install the `waku` command
cp .env.example .env                    # pick a provider, paste ONE key
uv run waku                             # talk to your Waku in the terminal
uv run waku dashboard                   # …or the browser cockpit → localhost:7777
uv run waku serve                       # …or always-on: it wakes for Telegram, Slack, GitHub and timers

To run the evals, install the test extras first. make eval then runs the offline checks with no API key:

uv pip install -e ".[dev,eval,hosted]"
make eval

Now try it. "Remember that Alex prefers morning meetings." Quit. Restart. "Book a catch-up with Alex on Friday." → it remembers, and books 9am. Your memory is one file: ~/.waku/state.db, the same from every folder.

Use the model you already pay for. Anthropic (default), OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Kimi, GLM, OpenRouter (one key, hundreds of hosted models), OpenCode Zen, or OpenCode Go — set WAKU_PROVIDER=, paste the key, done. One dialect in the loop; a ~60-line adapter handles the rest.

New to it? Getting started walks the whole setup, with a check at the end of every step.
